claims.claim: SPRiNT parameterized spectrograms were better fits to ground truth (MAE = 0.04) than those from wavelet-specparam (MAE = 0.58) in simulation challenge I.
claims.source: Overall, we found that SPRiNT parameterized spectrograms were better fits to ground truth (MAE = 0.04 and SEM = 2.9 × 10–5) than those from wavelet-specparam (MAE = 0.58 and SEM = 5.1 × 10–6; Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulation studies, shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: SPRiNT showed marked differences in performance compared to wavelet-specparam in the parameterization of aperiodic components.
claims.source: The data showed marked differences in performance between SPRiNT and wavelet-specparam in the parameterization of aperiodic components (error on aperiodic spectrogram: wavelet-specparam MAE = 0.60 and SEM = 6.7 × 10–6; SPRiNT MAE = 0.06 and SEM = 4.0 × 10–5).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from simulation studies.

claims.claim: The performances of SPRiNT and wavelet-specparam in parameterizing periodic components were strong and similar.
claims.source: The performances of the two methods in parameterizing periodic components were strong and similar (wavelet-specparam MAE = 0.05 and SEM = 4.0 × 10–6; SPRiNT MAE = 0.03 and SEM = 2.7 × 10–5).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from simulation studies.

claims.claim: SPRiNT detected periodic alpha activity with higher sensitivity (99%) and specificity (96%) than wavelet-specparam (95% sensitivity and 47% specificity).
claims.source: SPRiNT detected periodic alpha activity with higher sensitivity (99% at time bins with maximum peak amplitude) and specificity (96%) than wavelet-specparam (95% sensitivity and 47% specificity).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulation studies comparing detection performance.

claims.claim: SPRiNT estimates of alpha-peak parameters were closer to ground truth than wavelet-specparam's estimates.
claims.source: SPRiNT estimates of alpha-peak parameters were also closer to ground truth (centre frequency, amplitude, and bandwidth MAE [SEM] = 0.33 [3.6 × 10–4] Hz, 0.20 [1.7 × 10–4] a.u., and 0.42 [4.8 × 10–4] Hz, respectively) than wavelet-specparam's (MAE [SEM]=0.41 Hz [4.8 × 10–5], 0.24 [2.6 × 10–5] a.u., and 0.64 [6.4 × 10–5] Hz, respectively; Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from simulation studies, shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: SPRiNT detected and tracked down-chirping beta periodic activity with higher sensitivity (95%) and specificity (98%) than wavelet-specparam (62% sensitivity and 90% specificity).
claims.source: SPRiNT detected and tracked down-chirping beta periodic activity with higher sensitivity (95% at time bins with maximum peak amplitude) and specificity (98%) than wavelet-specparam (62% sensitivity and 90% specificity).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulation studies comparing detection performance.

claims.claim: Both SPRiNT and wavelet-specparam tended to overestimate peak bandwidths.
claims.source: We noted that both methods tended to overestimate peak bandwidths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and the effect was more pronounced with wavelet-specparam (Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from simulation studies, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2c.

claims.claim: SPRiNT and wavelet-specparam performances varied with the chosen parameters (spectral/temporal resolutions).
claims.source: While SPRiNT and wavelet-specparam performances varied with the chosen parameters (i.e., spectral/temporal resolutions; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3; see Supplemental materials), the optimal settings for SPRiNT outperformed the optimal settings for wavelet-specparam.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in supplemental figures showing parameter sensitivity analyses.

claims.claim: The optimal settings for SPRiNT outperformed the optimal settings for wavelet-specparam.
claims.source: While SPRiNT and wavelet-specparam performances varied with the chosen parameters (i.e., spectral/temporal resolutions; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3; see Supplemental materials), the optimal settings for SPRiNT outperformed the optimal settings for wavelet-specparam.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparative analyses across different parameter settings.

claims.claim: Specparam detected only the alpha peak (99% sensitivity) and no beta peaks across all spectra in simulation challenge I.
claims.source: The only peak detected by specparam (99% sensitivity) was the alpha peak, with an average centre frequency of 8.09 Hz (actual = 8 Hz), amplitude of 0.79 a.u. (actual max = 1.2 a.u.), and peak frequency SD of 1.21 Hz (actual = 1.2 Hz). No beta peaks were detected across all spectra processed with specparam.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying specparam to simulated data.

claims.claim: SPRiNT recovered 69% of the simulated periodic components with 89% specificity in simulation challenge II.
claims.source: SPRiNT, followed by outlier peak post-processing, recovered 69% of the simulated periodic components, with 89% specificity (70% sensitivity and 73% specificity prior to outlier removal as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulation challenge II.

claims.claim: In simulation challenge II, aperiodic exponent and offset parameters were recovered with MAEs of 0.12 and 0.15, respectively.
claims.source: Aperiodic exponent and offset parameters were recovered with MAEs of 0.12 and 0.15, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulation challenge II.

claims.claim: In simulation challenge II, the centre frequency, amplitude, and frequency width of periodic components were recovered with MAEs of 0.45, 0.23, and 0.49, respectively.
claims.source: The centre frequency, amplitude, and frequency width of periodic components were recovered with MAEs of 0.45, 0.23, and 0.49, respectively (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulation challenge II, shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: SPRiNT accurately detects up to two simultaneous periodic components.
claims.source: The synthesized data showed that overall, SPRiNT accurately detects up to two simultaneous periodic components (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulation challenge II, shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: Periodic components of lower frequencies were more challenging for SPRiNT to detect.
claims.source: We also found that periodic components of lower frequencies were more challenging to detect (Figure 3c,d; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) because their peak spectral component, when present, tended to be masked by the aperiodic component of the power spectrum.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from simulation challenge II, shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Lower amplitude peaks were more challenging for SPRiNT to detect.
claims.source: We also observed that lower amplitude peaks were more challenging to detect (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from simulation challenge II, shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: The detection rate in SPRiNT did not depend on peak bandwidth.
claims.source: However, the detection rate did not depend on peak bandwidth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulation challenge II, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: When two or more peaks were present simultaneously, the detection of either or both peaks depended on their spectral proximity.
claims.source: We found that when two or more peaks were present simultaneously, the detection of either or both peaks depended on their spectral proximity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulation challenge II, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Model fit errors varied significantly with the number of simultaneous periodic components, but this effect was small.
claims.source: Model fit errors (MAE = 0.032) varied significantly with the number of simultaneous periodic components, but this effect was small (β = –0.0001, SE = 6.7 × 10–6, 95% CI [−0.0001 to 0.0001], p=8.6 × 10–85; R2 = 0.0003; Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from simulation challenge II, shown in Figure 3e.

claims.claim: Group-averaged periodograms showed increased Oz signal power in the alpha range (6–14 Hz) in the eyes-closed behavioural condition with respect to eyes-open.
claims.source: As expected, the group-averaged periodograms showed increased Oz signal power in the alpha range (6–14 Hz) in the eyes-closed behavioural condition with respect to eyes-open (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding from the LEMON dataset, shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Alpha-peak power (β = –2.73) and aperiodic exponent (β = 1.14) are predictors of eyes-open or eyes-closed behaviour based on specparam outputs.
claims.source: A logistic regression of specparam outputs (aperiodic exponent, alpha-peak centre frequency, and alpha-peak amplitude entered as fixed effects) identified alpha-peak power (β = –2.73, SE = 0.33, 95% CI [−3.42,–2.11]; Bayes Factor BF = 3.21 × 10–21) and aperiodic exponent (β = 1.14, SE = 0.42, 95% CI [0.33,–1.99]; BF = 0.20) as predictors of eyes-open or eyes-closed behaviour (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from logistic regression analysis of empirical EEG data.

claims.claim: Lower alpha power and larger aperiodic exponents characterize the eyes-open condition.
claims.source: The resulting model suggests that both lower alpha power and larger aperiodic exponents characterize the eyes-open condition.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the logistic regression results.

claims.claim: Sharp changes in aperiodic exponent and offset occur at the transitions between eyes-open and eyes-closed, which are likely artefactual residuals of eye movements.
claims.source: We observed sharp changes in aperiodic exponent and offset at the transitions between eyes-open and eyes-closed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which are likely to be artefactual residuals of eye movements.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from SPRiNT analysis of empirical data, with an interpretation about the source of the effect.

claims.claim: Mean alpha power (β = –6.31), SD of alpha power (β = 4.64), and mean aperiodic exponent (β = 2.55) are significant predictors of behavioural condition (eyes-open vs eyes-closed) based on SPRiNT parameters.
claims.source: We ran a logistic regression model with SPRiNT parameter estimates as fixed effects (mean and SD of alpha centre frequency, alpha power, and the aperiodic exponent across time) and found a significant effect of mean alpha power (β = –6.31, SE = 0.92, and 95% CI [–8.23,–4.61]), SD of alpha power (β = 4.64, SE = 2.03, and 95% CI [0.76, 8.73]), and mean aperiodic exponent (β = 2.55, SE = 0.53, and 95% CI [1.55, 3.63]) as predictors of the behavioural condition (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from logistic regression analysis using SPRiNT parameters.

claims.claim: Lower alpha power, larger aperiodic exponents, and stronger fluctuations of alpha-band activity over time are signatures of the eyes-open resting condition.
claims.source: According to this model, lower alpha power, larger aperiodic exponents, and stronger fluctuations of alpha-band activity over time are signatures of the eyes-open resting condition.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the logistic regression results using SPRiNT parameters.

claims.claim: Bayes factor analysis confirmed the evidence of effects of mean alpha power (BF = 4.39 × 10–13) and mean aperiodic exponent (BF = 1.62 × 10–4) on behavioral condition.
claims.source: A Bayes factor analysis confirmed the evidence of effects of mean alpha power (BF = 4.39 × 10–13) and mean aperiodic exponent (BF = 1.62 × 10–4), and indicated mild evidence against the temporal variability of alpha power (BF = 3.81; Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayes factor analysis.

claims.claim: Bayes factor analysis indicated mild evidence against the temporal variability of alpha power (BF = 3.81) as a predictor of behavioral condition.
claims.source: A Bayes factor analysis confirmed the evidence of effects of mean alpha power (BF = 4.39 × 10–13) and mean aperiodic exponent (BF = 1.62 × 10–4), and indicated mild evidence against the temporal variability of alpha power (BF = 3.81; Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayes factor analysis.

claims.claim: Both specparam and SPRiNT analyses confirmed alpha power and aperiodic exponent as neurophysiological markers of eyes-closed vs eyes-open behaviour.
claims.source: In summary, both specparam and SPRiNT analyses confirmed alpha power and aperiodic exponent as neurophysiological markers of eyes-closed vs eyes-open behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the empirical analyses.

claims.claim: SPRiNT's spectrogram parameterization was uniquely able to reveal time-varying changes in alpha power related to eyes-closed vs eyes-open behaviour.
claims.source: We emphasize that SPRiNT's spectrogram parameterization was uniquely able to reveal time-varying changes in alpha power related to eyes-closed vs eyes-open behaviour, although the Bayes factor for this effect suggests it to be marginal.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about SPRiNT's unique capabilities, with a caveat about the strength of evidence.

claims.claim: Mean aperiodic exponent (β = –3.31) and SD of alpha centre frequency (β = 1.30) are significant predictors of age group in the eyes-open condition based on SPRiNT parameters.
claims.source: We found significant effects of mean aperiodic exponent (β = –3.31, SE = 0.75, and 95% CI [−4.88,–1.91]) and SD of alpha centre frequency (β = 1.30, SE = 0.53, and 95% CI [0.28, 2.39]; Table 5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from logistic regression predicting age group.

claims.claim: The EEG spectrogram of older participants decreased less rapidly with frequency (characterized by a smaller exponent) and revealed stronger time-varying fluctuations of alpha-peak centre frequency.
claims.source: We therefore found using SPRiNT that the EEG spectrogram of older participants decreased less rapidly with frequency (characterized by a smaller exponent) and revealed stronger time-varying fluctuations of alpha-peak centre frequency.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the logistic regression results for age prediction.

claims.claim: Bayes factor analysis showed strong evidence for the effect of the aperiodic exponent (BF = 5.14 × 10–5) and for the variability of the alpha-peak centre frequency (BF = 0.20) on age group in the eyes-open condition.
claims.source: A Bayes factor analysis showed strong evidence for the effect of the aperiodic exponent (BF = 5.14 × 10–5) and for the variability of the alpha-peak centre frequency (BF = 0.20; Table 5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayes factor analysis.

claims.claim: Mean aperiodic exponent (β = –4.34) and mean alpha centre frequency (β = –0.74) are predictors of participants' age group in the eyes-closed condition based on SPRiNT parameters.
claims.source: We found that mean aperiodic exponent (β = –4.34, SE = 0.84, and 95% CI [−6.10,–2.79]) and mean alpha centre frequency (β = –0.74, SE = 0.27, and 95% CI [−1.28,–0.24]) were predictors of participants' age group, with older participants again showing a flatter spectrum and a slower alpha peak (lower centre frequency; Table 6).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from logistic regression predicting age group in the eyes-closed condition.

claims.claim: Older participants show a flatter spectrum and a slower alpha peak (lower centre frequency) in the eyes-closed condition.
claims.source: We found that mean aperiodic exponent (β = –4.34, SE = 0.84, and 95% CI [−6.10,–2.79]) and mean alpha centre frequency (β = –0.74, SE = 0.27, and 95% CI [−1.28,–0.24]) were predictors of participants' age group, with older participants again showing a flatter spectrum and a slower alpha peak (lower centre frequency; Table 6).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the logistic regression results.

claims.claim: Bayes factor analysis provided strong evidence for the effect of mean aperiodic exponent (BF = 1.10 × 10–7) and for the effect of mean alpha centre frequency (BF = 0.07) on age group in the eyes-closed condition.
claims.source: A Bayes factor analysis provided strong evidence for the effect of mean aperiodic exponent (BF = 1.10 × 10–7) and for the effect of mean alpha centre frequency (BF = 0.07; Table 6).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayes factor analysis.

claims.claim: Resting bouts in rats were associated with larger aperiodic exponents and more positive offsets than during movement bouts.
claims.source: SPRiNT parameterization found in the two subjects that resting bouts were associated with larger aperiodic exponents and more positive offsets than during movement bouts (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from SPRiNT analysis of rodent intracranial data, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Dynamic shifts between aperiodic modes were observed in rats associated with behavioural changes between movement and rest.
claims.source: We ran SPRiNT parameterizations over 8 s epochs proximal to transitions between movement and rest; we observed dynamic shifts between aperiodic modes associated with behavioural changes (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from SPRiNT analysis of rodent data, shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Changes in aperiodic exponent proximal to transitions of movement and rest were negatively associated with movement speed in both rat subjects for both transition types.
claims.source: We tested whether changes in aperiodic exponent proximal to transitions of movement and rest were related to movement speed and found a negative linear association in both subjects for both transition types (EC012 transitions to rest: β = –9.6 × 10–3, SE = 4.7 × 10–4, 95% CI [–1.1 × 10–2 –8.6 × 10–3], p<0.001, R2 = 0.29; EC012 transitions to movement: β = –7.3 × 10–3, SE = 4.3 × 10–4, 95% CI [–8.1 × 10–3 –6.4 × 10–3], p<0.001, R2 = 0.18; EC013 transitions to rest: β = –1.1 × 10–2, SE = 2.3 × 10–4, 95% CI [–1.2x10–2 –1.1x10–2], p<0.001, R2 = 0.32; EC013 transitions to movement: β = –1.2 × 10–2, SE = 3.2 × 10–4, 95% CI [–1.3x10–2 –1.2x10–2], p<0.001, R2 = 0.26; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear regression analysis of rodent data.

claims.claim: The smaller aperiodic exponents observed during movement in rats may be indicative of periods of general cortical disinhibition.
claims.source: The smaller aperiodic exponents observed during movement may be indicative of periods of general cortical disinhibition (Gao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the rodent data findings, supported by citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Changes in aperiodic exponent in rats could reflect increased processing demands from additional spatial information entering entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: Changes in aperiodic exponent were partially explained by movement speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which could reflect increased processing demands from additional spatial information entering entorhinal cortex (Keene et al., 2016) or increased activity in cells encoding speed directly (Iwase et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citations to Keene et al., 2016 and Iwase et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Changes in aperiodic exponent in rats could reflect increased activity in cells encoding speed directly.
claims.source: Changes in aperiodic exponent were partially explained by movement speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which could reflect increased processing demands from additional spatial information entering entorhinal cortex (Keene et al., 2016) or increased activity in cells encoding speed directly (Iwase et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citation to Iwase et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Aperiodic background neural activity changes in relation to a variety of contexts and subject types.
claims.source: Combined, the reported findings support the notion that aperiodic background neural activity changes in relation to a variety of contexts and subject types (Donoghue et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2017; Molina et al., 2020; Ostlund et al., 2021; Pathania et al., 2021; Waschke et al., 2021; van Heumen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: SPRiNT extends the approach to the low-dimensional time-resolved parameterization of neurophysiological spectrograms.
claims.source: SPRiNT extends the approach to the low-dimensional time-resolved parameterization of neurophysiological spectrograms.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological contribution of SPRiNT.

claims.claim: SPRiNT combines the simplicity of the specparam spectral decomposition approach with the computational efficiency of STFTs across sliding windows.
claims.source: The method combines the simplicity of the specparam spectral decomposition approach with the computational efficiency of STFTs across sliding windows.
claims.evidence: This describes the design principles of SPRiNT.

claims.claim: SPRiNT unveils meaningful additional information from the data beyond established tools such as wavelet time-frequency decompositions.
claims.source: The present results demonstrate its technical concept and indicate that SPRiNT unveils meaningful additional information from the data beyond established tools such as wavelet time-frequency decompositions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analyses presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: SPRiNT performs optimally when the data features narrow-band oscillatory components that can be characterized as spectral peaks.
claims.source: We note that the algorithm performs optimally when the data features narrow-band oscillatory components that can be characterized as spectral peaks (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about SPRiNT's performance characteristics based on simulation studies.

claims.claim: SPRiNT performs best when the data contains two or fewer salient periodic components concurrently.
claims.source: The algorithm performs best when the data contains two or fewer salient periodic components concurrently (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about SPRiNT's performance characteristics based on simulation studies.

claims.claim: The current limitations of SPRiNT in detecting spectral peaks at the lower edge of the power spectrum are inherent to specparam.
claims.source: We found that these current limitations are inherent to specparam, which is challenged by the dissociation of spectral peaks from background aperiodic activity at the lower edge of the power spectrum (Donoghue et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the source of SPRiNT's limitations, supported by citation to Donoghue et al., 2020.

claims.claim: SPRiNT tends to overestimate the bandwidth of spectral peaks, which is related to the frequency resolution of the spectrogram.
claims.source: The algorithm tends to overestimate the bandwidth of spectral peaks, which we discuss as related to the frequency resolution of the spectrogram (mostly 1 Hz in the present study).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from simulation studies with an interpretation about the cause.

claims.claim: The intrinsic noise level present in STFTs may challenge bandwidth estimation in SPRiNT.
claims.source: The intrinsic noise level present in STFTs (i.e., spectral power not explained by periodic or aperiodic components) may also challenge bandwidth estimation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about a factor affecting SPRiNT's performance.

claims.claim: Increasing STFT window length augments spectral resolution and reduces intrinsic noise, although to the detriment of temporal specificity.
claims.source: Increasing STFT window length augments spectral resolution and reduces intrinsic noise, although to the detriment of temporal specificity.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the trade-offs in STFT parameter selection, based on signal processing knowledge.

claims.claim: SPRiNT may underestimate the number of periodic components, which can be interpreted as the joint probability of detecting multiple independent oscillatory peaks.
claims.source: We also found that SPRiNT may underestimate the number of periodic components, though this can be interpreted as the joint probability of SPRiNT detecting multiple independent oscillatory peaks (where the probability of detecting a given peak is between 65 and 75%; approximating a binomial distribution).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from simulation studies with a statistical interpretation.

claims.claim: A peak was more likely to be detected by SPRiNT if its amplitude is stronger and the centre frequency is above 8 Hz.
claims.source: We found that a peak was more likely to be detected if its amplitude is stronger and the centre frequency is above 8 Hz (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), and if separated from other peaks by at least 8 Hz (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulation studies shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: A peak was more likely to be detected by SPRiNT if separated from other peaks by at least 8 Hz.
claims.source: We found that a peak was more likely to be detected if its amplitude is stronger and the centre frequency is above 8 Hz (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), and if separated from other peaks by at least 8 Hz (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulation studies shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: SPRiNT's performances were slightly degraded when spectrograms composed an aperiodic knee.
claims.source: Finally, SPRiNT's performances were slightly degraded when spectrograms composed an aperiodic knee (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulation studies shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The spectral knee frequency is related to intrinsic neuronal timescales and cortical microarchitecture.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the spectral knee frequency is related to intrinsic neuronal timescales and cortical microarchitecture (Gao et al., 2020), which are expected to be stable properties within each individual and across a given recording.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The spectral knee frequency is expected to be a stable property within each individual and across a given recording.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the spectral knee frequency is related to intrinsic neuronal timescales and cortical microarchitecture (Gao et al., 2020), which are expected to be stable properties within each individual and across a given recording.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the physiological interpretation of the knee parameter.

claims.claim: SPRiNT's optional outlier peak removal procedure increases the specificity of detected spectral peaks by emphasizing the detection of periodic components that develop over time.
claims.source: SPRiNT's optional outlier peak removal procedure increases the specificity of detected spectral peaks by emphasizing the detection of periodic components that develop over time.
claims.evidence: This describes the purpose and effect of the outlier removal procedure.

claims.claim: Applying a semi-conservative threshold for outlier removal reduced the false detection rate by 50%, without affecting the true detection rate substantially (a<5% reduction).
claims.source: So far, we found that applying a semi-conservative threshold for outlier removal (i.e., if less than three more peaks are detected within 2.5 Hz and 3 s around a given peak of the spectrogram) reduced the false detection rate by 50%, without affecting the true detection rate substantially (a<5% reduction; Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result about the effect of the outlier removal procedure.

claims.claim: Setting outlier removal threshold parameters too conservatively would reduce the sensitivity of peak detection.
claims.source: Setting these threshold parameters too conservatively would reduce the sensitivity of peak detection.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the trade-offs in parameter selection.

claims.claim: Baseline normalization followed by narrow-band analysis of power changes is not immune to interpretation ambiguities when aperiodic background activity also changes dynamically.
claims.source: However, the resulting relative measures of event-related power increases or decreases do not explicitly account for the fact that behaviour or stimulus presentations may also induce rapid changes in aperiodic activity. Therefore, baseline normalization followed by narrow-band analysis of power changes is not immune to interpretation ambiguities when aperiodic background activity also changes dynamically.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of baseline normalization methods.

claims.claim: Measuring narrow band power changes without accounting for concurrent variations of the aperiodic signal background challenges the interpretation of effects manifested in the spectrogram.
claims.source: We found in the LEMON dataset that measuring narrow band power changes without accounting for concurrent variations of the aperiodic signal background challenges the interpretation of effects manifested in the spectrogram (Scally et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the empirical analysis, supported by citation to Scally et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Spectral parameterization with SPRiNT or specparam enables the distinction between periodic and aperiodic changes in neural activity.
claims.source: Spectral parameterization with SPRiNT or specparam enables this distinction, showing that both periodic and aperiodic changes in neural activity are associated with age and behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of spectral parameterization methods.

claims.claim: It remains unclear whether the effects of alpha-peak power and aperiodic exponent on behavioral condition are independent or related.
claims.source: However, it remains unclear whether these effects are independent or related.
claims.evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: The amplitude of alpha oscillations around a non-zero mean voltage influences baseline cortical excitability.
claims.source: A recent analysis of the same dataset showed that the amplitude of alpha oscillations around a non-zero mean voltage influences baseline cortical excitability (Studenova et al., 2021)—an effect observable in part through variations of the aperiodic exponent (Gao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Studenova et al., 2021 and Gao et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Using both SPRiNT and specparam, slower alpha-peak centre frequencies and smaller aperiodic exponents were observed in the older age group, in agreement with previous literature on healthy ageing.
claims.source: Using both SPRiNT and specparam, we also observed both slower alpha-peak centre frequencies and smaller aperiodic exponents in the older age group, in agreement with previous literature on healthy ageing (Cellier et al., 2021; Donoghue et al., 2020; Hill et al., 2022; Ostlund et al., 2022; Schaworonkow and Voytek, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Using specparam, lower alpha-band peak amplitudes were found in older individuals in the eyes-closed condition.
claims.source: Using specparam, we found lower alpha-band peak amplitudes in older individuals in the eyes-closed condition.
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding from specparam analysis.

claims.claim: The effect of lower alpha-band peak amplitudes in older individuals could not be replicated from spectrograms parameterized with SPRiNT.
claims.source: We could not replicate this effect from spectrograms parameterized with SPRiNT (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding showing a difference between specparam and SPRiNT results.

claims.claim: The apparent divergence between specparam and SPRiNT in detecting alpha-peak amplitude effects may be due to the challenge of detecting low-amplitude peaks in the spectrogram of older individuals.
claims.source: This apparent divergence may be due to the challenge of detecting low-amplitude peaks in the spectrogram of older individuals.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for the divergence in results.

claims.claim: Periodograms are derived from averaging across time windows, which augments signal-to-noise ratios, and therefore the sensitivity of specparam to periodic components of lower amplitude.
claims.source: Periodograms are derived from averaging across time windows, which augments signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), and therefore the sensitivity of specparam to periodic components of lower amplitude.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation based on signal processing principles.

claims.claim: In a subset of participants (<10%), considerable differences were observed between the alpha-peak amplitudes extracted from specparam and SPRiNT, explained by unstable expressions of alpha activity over time.
claims.source: In a subset of participants (<10%), we also observed considerable differences between the alpha-peak amplitudes extracted from specparam and SPRiNT, which we explained by unstable expressions of alpha activity over time in these participants (Figure 4c).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from empirical data with an interpretation, shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: The average alpha-peak amplitude estimated with SPRiNT is based only on time segments when an alpha-band periodic component is detected.
claims.source: The average alpha-peak amplitude estimated with SPRiNT is based only on time segments when an alpha-band periodic component is detected.

results.result: SPRiNT is a novel method that combines short-time Fourier transforms (STFTs) with specparam to produce time-resolved parameterization of neural spectrograms, decomposing them into aperiodic and periodic components. The method includes an optional outlier removal procedure to increase specificity of detected spectral peaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C33-C37 provide a clear methodological description of SPRiNT, which is the core contribution of the manuscript. The method is well-defined with explicit steps (STFT computation, averaging, parameterization with specparam, optional outlier removal) and is demonstrated with both synthetic and empirical data throughout the paper.

results.result: In simulation challenge I with transient and chirping periodic components, SPRiNT outperformed wavelet-specparam in recovering time-varying spectral features, particularly for aperiodic components (MAE=0.06 vs 0.60) and showed higher sensitivity and specificity for detecting alpha (99%/96% vs 95%/47%) and beta peaks (95%/98% vs 62%/90%).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C46 provide comprehensive quantitative comparisons with specific MAE values, sensitivity/specificity metrics, and statistical measures across 10,000 simulations. The results consistently demonstrate SPRiNT's superior performance, with appropriate acknowledgment of limitations (both methods overestimate peak bandwidths). The comparison is rigorous and well-documented.

results.result: In simulation challenge II with randomly generated realistic parameters, SPRiNT recovered 69% of simulated periodic components with 89% specificity, accurately detecting up to two simultaneous periodic components. Performance was affected by peak frequency (lower frequencies more challenging), amplitude (lower amplitudes harder to detect), and spectral proximity (peaks needed >8 Hz separation).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C56 provide detailed quantitative performance metrics from 10,000 heterogeneous simulations with specific MAE values for all parameters. The characterization of limitations is thorough and honest, identifying specific conditions affecting detection (frequency, amplitude, proximity). The small effect of number of peaks on model fit (R²=0.0003) is appropriately noted as negligible.

results.result: In resting-state EEG data (n=178), both specparam and SPRiNT identified alpha power and aperiodic exponent as predictors of eyes-open vs eyes-closed behavior. SPRiNT uniquely revealed that temporal variability of alpha power also predicts behavioral condition, though Bayes factor analysis indicated this effect was marginal (BF=3.81).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C66 present convergent evidence from both specparam and SPRiNT analyses with appropriate statistical tests (logistic regression, Bayes factors). The unique contribution of SPRiNT (temporal variability) is identified but appropriately qualified as marginal based on Bayes factor analysis. The sample size (n=178) is adequate and the statistical approach is sound.

results.result: SPRiNT analysis of resting-state EEG revealed that older adults (55-80 years) show smaller aperiodic exponents (flatter spectra), slower alpha-peak center frequencies, and greater temporal variability in alpha-peak center frequency during eyes-open condition compared to younger adults (20-40 years), consistent with previous literature on healthy aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 and C103 provide consistent findings across both eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions with appropriate statistical support (logistic regression with confidence intervals, Bayes factors showing strong evidence). The results align with cited prior literature, providing convergent validity. The sample sizes (younger n=121, older n=57) are adequate for the analyses performed.

results.result: In rodent intracranial recordings, SPRiNT revealed that resting bouts were associated with larger aperiodic exponents and more positive offsets than movement bouts, with dynamic shifts observed at behavioral transitions. Changes in aperiodic exponent were negatively associated with movement speed (R²=0.18-0.32, p<0.001 for all transitions), potentially reflecting cortical disinhibition during movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 present consistent findings across two rat subjects with appropriate statistical analyses (linear regression with confidence intervals and R² values). The negative association with movement speed is well-documented. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C76 - cortical disinhibition) is appropriately qualified as speculative and supported only by citation, not direct measurement.

results.result: When applied to simulation challenge I data, specparam (analyzing static periodograms) detected only the alpha peak with 99% sensitivity and failed to detect any beta peaks, demonstrating the limitation of static spectral analysis for time-varying signals.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 provides a clear quantitative result demonstrating the limitation of static spectral parameterization. This serves as an important control showing that time-resolved methods are necessary for capturing transient spectral features. The result directly supports the motivation for SPRiNT.

results.result: SPRiNT performs optimally with narrow-band oscillatory components and ≤2 simultaneous periodic components. Current limitations include: overestimation of peak bandwidths (related to 1 Hz frequency resolution), underestimation of number of peaks (65-75% detection probability per peak), difficulty detecting peaks <8 Hz or with amplitudes below threshold, and slightly degraded performance with aperiodic knees.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C92 provide an honest and thorough characterization of SPRiNT's limitations based on simulation studies. The limitations are quantified where possible and mechanistic explanations are provided (e.g., frequency resolution, masking by aperiodic component). This transparency about method limitations is appropriate and well-supported by the simulation data.

results.result: SPRiNT's optional outlier peak removal procedure (requiring ≥3 similar peaks within 2.5 Hz and 3 s) reduced false detection rate by 50% with minimal impact on true detection rate (<5% reduction), though overly conservative thresholds would reduce sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide quantitative assessment of the outlier removal procedure's performance with specific metrics. The trade-off between specificity and sensitivity is appropriately acknowledged. The procedure is optional and its effects are well-characterized, allowing users to make informed decisions.

results.result: Specparam detected lower alpha-peak amplitudes in older individuals during eyes-closed condition, but this effect could not be replicated with SPRiNT. This divergence may reflect differences in how the methods calculate average amplitude: specparam averages across all time windows while SPRiNT only includes time segments with detected alpha peaks, making SPRiNT sensitive to temporal instability of alpha activity observed in <10% of participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C111 identify a discrepancy between methods and provide a plausible mechanistic explanation based on methodological differences. The explanation is logical and supported by observation of temporal instability in a subset of participants (Figure 4c). However, the speculation about low-amplitude peak detection (C106) is less certain. The overall interpretation is reasonable but acknowledges uncertainty.

results.result: SPRiNT demonstrates specific strengths compared to wavelet-specparam approaches, particularly in recovering aperiodic signal components. Wavelet-specparam underperformed and required substantial temporal smoothing (4 s Gaussian kernel) to achieve error levels similar to SPRiNT, yielding redundancy in spectral parameterization.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C82, C124-C125 are well-supported by the comparative analyses in simulation studies. The quantitative differences in performance are documented (C38-C39), and the need for extensive smoothing in wavelet-specparam is demonstrated. This establishes SPRiNT's practical advantages over an alternative approach.

results.result: Baseline normalization methods for spectrograms are not immune to interpretation ambiguities when aperiodic background activity changes dynamically. Spectral parameterization with SPRiNT or specparam enables distinction between periodic and aperiodic changes, showing both are associated with age and behavior in the LEMON dataset.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 identify a conceptual limitation of traditional approaches and demonstrate how spectral parameterization addresses it. The empirical support comes from the LEMON dataset analyses (C57-C72) showing distinct contributions of periodic and aperiodic components. The argument is logical and well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: Temporal variability of spectral parameters relates to demographic features, as demonstrated by SPRiNT's ability to predict age from temporal variability of eyes-open alpha-peak center frequency. This suggests temporal variability of neural spectral features may be neurophysiologically significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 present an interesting finding about temporal variability predicting age (C67-C69), supported by appropriate statistics. However, C115 is appropriately qualified as speculative. The result opens new research directions but the mechanistic significance remains to be established. The finding is novel and well-documented but requires further investigation.

results.result: Current understanding establishes that neural dynamics comprise aperiodic (1/f) and periodic components representing distinct physiological mechanisms. While recent advances enable spectral parameterization, current methods yield static decompositions despite neural signals varying dynamically. Baseline normalization assumes stable aperiodic characteristics, an assumption challenged by recent evidence of temporal fluctuations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10, C13-C17, C25-C28, C32 establish the scientific context and motivation for SPRiNT. These are well-supported by appropriate citations to established literature. The claims accurately represent current knowledge and identify a genuine gap (lack of time-resolved parameterization) that SPRiNT addresses. This provides strong justification for the work.

results.result: Aperiodic parameters have established physiological interpretations: offset reflects neuronal population spiking, exponent relates to synaptic current integration and E/I balance (larger exponent indicates stronger inhibition). Aperiodic activity is ubiquitous in the brain and differentiates healthy aging, with potential as a marker for neuropsychiatric conditions and epilepsy.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C24, C93, C102, C119 summarize established knowledge about aperiodic activity, appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. These claims provide important context for interpreting SPRiNT results but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations are consistent with the cited work.

results.result: STFT offers computational efficiency but is less sophisticated than wavelet alternatives in trading off temporal specificity and frequency resolution. Combining specparam with STFT yields rapid extraction of spectral parameters. While spectral parameterization could supplement any time-frequency decomposition technique, reduced computational cost remains a practical benefit of STFT.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123, C126 provide appropriate context about the trade-offs in choosing STFT for SPRiNT. The characterization of STFT's advantages (computational efficiency) and limitations (fixed time-frequency resolution) is accurate and supported by citation to Cohen, 2014. The practical justification for the design choice is reasonable.

results.result: Sharp changes in aperiodic exponent and offset occur at transitions between eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions in the LEMON dataset, likely representing artefactual residuals of eye movements rather than genuine neural dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 identifies a potential artifact in the data and provides a reasonable interpretation. The observation is documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and the interpretation (eye movement artifacts) is plausible given the timing at behavioral transitions. The authors appropriately excluded these segments (2.5 s centered at transitions) from further analysis, demonstrating good experimental practice.

results.result: Changes in aperiodic exponent in rats during movement transitions could reflect either increased processing demands from additional spatial information entering entorhinal cortex or increased activity in cells encoding speed directly.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 present speculative mechanistic interpretations of the rodent findings, appropriately qualified with 'could reflect' and supported by citations to relevant literature (Keene et al., 2016; Iwase et al., 2020). However, these are post-hoc interpretations without direct experimental evidence. The speculation is reasonable but the claims cannot be considered supported without additional experiments to test these specific mechanisms.

results.result: SPRiNT provides estimates of dynamic fluctuations in aperiodic and periodic neural activity related to meaningful demographic and behavioral outcomes. The method could contribute to improving tools for detecting oscillatory bursts, and future developments may include model selection approaches based on Bayesian information criterion for determining periodic component parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 summarize the demonstrated capabilities of SPRiNT (C129 is well-supported by empirical results) and suggest future directions (C127-C128, C130). The demonstrated capabilities are well-supported by the data. The future directions are appropriately speculative and represent reasonable extensions of the work. C127 and C128 are suggestions rather than claims requiring validation.

results.result: Brain oscillations have been causally linked to behavior and cognition and shape sensory responses. Specparam sequentially fits aperiodic (exponent, offset) and periodic (Gaussian functions with center frequency, amplitude, SD) components to power spectra. Aperiodic background activity changes across various contexts and subject types, and strong theta activity may challenge aperiodic parameter estimation.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C29-C31, C79, C116-C118 provide background knowledge and methodological context, all appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. These establish the scientific foundation and known limitations that inform the interpretation of SPRiNT results. The characterizations are accurate representations of cited work.

results.result: Increasing STFT window length augments spectral resolution and reduces intrinsic noise, although at the detriment of temporal specificity.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 describes a fundamental trade-off in time-frequency analysis that is well-established in signal processing. This is general knowledge about STFT properties and represents an accurate characterization of the method's inherent limitations. The trade-off is relevant for understanding SPRiNT's parameter choices.

results.result: It remains unclear whether the effects of alpha-peak power and aperiodic exponent on behavioral condition (eyes-open vs eyes-closed) are independent or related.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 appropriately acknowledges a limitation in the interpretation of the LEMON dataset results. While both parameters predict behavioral condition, the manuscript does not establish whether they represent independent mechanisms or are interdependent. This honest acknowledgment of uncertainty is appropriate given the correlational nature of the analysis.

results.result: Beta-band power suppression during motor execution is due to sparser bursting activity rather than sustained decrease of beta-band activity, as shown in prior work.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 cites prior work (Sherman et al., 2016) to provide context for interpreting the temporal instability of alpha activity observed in some participants. This is an appropriate use of prior literature to support interpretation of the current findings. The claim accurately represents cited work and draws a relevant parallel.

results.result: The spectral knee frequency is expected to be a stable property within each individual and across a given recording, based on its relationship to intrinsic neuronal timescales and cortical microarchitecture.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 makes a reasonable inference based on the physiological interpretation of the knee parameter (C93, supported by Gao et al., 2020). If the knee reflects stable anatomical/physiological properties, temporal stability is a logical expectation. This inference is appropriately qualified and provides practical guidance for SPRiNT users regarding knee parameter estimation.
